title: Getting to Know: Zach Groshell
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio interviews Zach Groshell, author of Just Tell Them, about his move from progressive, discovery-based teaching to explicit instruction. Groshell describes realising that poor behaviour came from the method rather than the children, that visually impressive projects flattered evaluators while hiding shallow understanding, and that the 2006 Kirschner, Sweller and Clark paper on cognitive load explained his students' struggles. He argues explicit teaching is preventative and more equitable rather than a last resort, is not paint-by-numbers, and is especially powerful for disadvantaged students because of background knowledge and working memory. He also points to the inconsistency of teaching phonics systematically and maths by discovery in one classroom, and says good explicit lessons are interactive like a tennis match.
points: Groshell traces his shift from discovery methods to noticing that the method, not the children, produced disengagement, and that engaging-looking lessons concealed what students actually understood.
Cognitive load theory gave him an explanation for why insufficient guidance overwhelms working memory.
Explicit instruction is positioned as preventative and equitable, not a rescue after students fail, and is skilled work involving sequencing, spaced practice and interleaving.
It helps disadvantaged learners by supplying background knowledge and respecting slower information processing.
Good explicit teaching is interactive and scaffolded, not a return to old-fashioned lecturing.
quotes: That poster project was sort of for the leader, the evaluator, who was thinking, “This is awesome.” It had an aesthetic to it that was very groovy, and it was very pleasing to see that kind of buzz and that engagement. But I realized when I started asking questions, drilling in on their thinking about the math, that they didn't know the math at all in any sophisticated way. But the lesson looked good!

That would be an article by Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark in 2006, on the failure of constructivist and inquiry-based problem-based learning. I read that in my first PhD methods course. They described cognitive load theory, and I went, “Wait, so the fact that the kids aren't learning has an explanation from cognitive science? That material can be too complex? Not having enough guidance can lead to cognitive overload, and working memory will break down and they won't be able to store all of those thoughts in long-term memory?” That was my moment.

But there’s this whole feeling in the field that using explanation and modeling is a last resort as opposed to something that's preventative, something that actually is more equitable in terms of getting the information to everyone, rather than waiting until the same kids fail, and then stopping everybody and correcting them in a really quick and frustrated way because you're mad they didn't figure it out on their own.

It is this sort of idealized, romantic perspective that if we just set the conditions, they will bloom like flowers. And the truth doesn't sit well with people: The real truth is they’re more like blocks of marble and we need to form them into the masterpiece that they could be.

A lot of people that read this may come away thinking that I'm talking about old-fashioned lecturing, so the first thing to remember is how interactive and how engaging a very well-designed explicit instruction lesson is. It's saying just a few words and refraining from saying all the extraneous things that kids don't need to think about. It's asking kids to respond, to write, getting everybody to do the same thing at the same time. And as you go back and forth with the kids, like a tennis match, you're creating this really joyful learning experience.
